egress.terms: metered at 1 GB/month, which is 33.3 MiB/day

chaining: composes with an origin and no domain; the 1 GB monthly allowance is what stops it being the front of anything served.

evidence.proved: Data transfer out 1 GB/month, 20,000 HTTP requests/month, 5,000 TCP connections/month, 3 endpoints and one dev domain

endpoints are limited to http, https, tcp and tls

notes: The record merged rate and quota into one request-rate entry. The docs separate three kinds of limit and the rate row is a distinct constraint that binds before the monthly count on a burst. Replaces the note about the vocabulary with the ratio and the documented consequence.

extras.transit_note: the agent dials out and ngrok's edge relays the bytes, which is what the 1 GB monthly counter counts

binding_note: 1 GB per month is about 1,100 times below 1 TiB, so the byte quota fails first by three orders of magnitude. The docs state the consequence as an upgrade recommendation rather than a throttle: once a limit is hit or the credit is gone, the endpoints stop being always available and the recommendation is to move to pay-as-you-go.
interface_detail: ngrok http; the dev domain is <name>.ngrok-free.app
limits_note: the allowance is a byte volume over a period, which none of the six kinds names; the number is in egress.free_allowance and binding names per-ip-shaping as the nearest kind. counts of things, not rates, so no vocabulary kind names them: 3 online endpoints and one dev domain per account
